conventional_description: In Western medicine, a sensation of a lump in the chest without an actual palpable mass is often called globus sensation or functional chest pain. It is frequently linked to anxiety, acid reflux, esophageal motility disorders, or muscle tension. Diagnostic tests like endoscopy or imaging may be normal, leaving patients frustrated. Treatment typically focuses on symptom management with antacids, muscle relaxants, or anxiety medications, but the sensation often returns with stress or dietary triggers.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment often includes proton pump inhibitors for suspected reflux, low-dose antidepressants for visceral hypersensitivity, or cognitive behavioral therapy for stress-related globus. If no physical cause is found, reassurance and lifestyle modifications are the mainstay.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the chest is a vital crossroads where the Qi of the Stomach, Spleen, Liver, and Lungs meet. The Stomach is meant to send its Qi downward - when it rebels and stagnates instead, you feel a stuck, full sensation that can register as a lump. This is why so many chest lumps are tied to digestion: the middle burner (the Stomach and Spleen system) is the engine that moves Qi through the torso.
The Liver is the other key player. It governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. Stress, frustration, or bottled-up anger can knot the Liver Qi, causing it to attack the Stomach and block the chest. That’s the classic stress-triggered lump - it comes with sighing, rib-side tension, and a wiry pulse. But there are other mechanisms too: when the Spleen is weak, fluids accumulate into Phlegm-Dampness that physically clogs the middle burner, creating a heavy, phlegmy lump that worsens after eating.
Deficiency patterns tell a different story. If the Spleen and Stomach lack the Qi to move food downward, turbid Qi rises and stagnates - the lump feels dull and eases with warmth and rest. If Stomach Yin runs dry, a subtle heat develops, and the lump becomes a nagging, burning sensation with thirst and a red, peeled tongue. In TCM, these are not one disease but six distinct imbalances, each with its own treatment.
classical_quote: 「心下痞，按之濡，其脉关上浮者，大黄黄连泻心汤主之。」
classical_translation: "When there is a lump sensation in the chest (epigastrium) that feels soft on palpation and the pulse is floating at the guan position, Da Huang Huang Lian Xie Xin Tang governs."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner starts by asking what the “lump” actually feels like - is it a tight knot, a heavy pressure, or a burning fullness - and when it appears. The timing and triggers are the first clues. A sensation that flares with anger points in a very different direction than one that comes on after a heavy meal or one that eases with warmth.
If the chest lump is clearly tied to emotional stress, frustration, or bottled-up anger, the practitioner looks toward Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. The person may sigh often, feel a distending pain that radiates to the ribs, and belch frequently. The tongue is often pale or slightly red with a thin white coating, and the pulse feels wiry, like a taut guitar string.
When the lump comes with a bitter taste in the mouth, nausea, a heavy body, and sticky stools, Damp-Heat in the Stomach and Spleen is the likely picture. This often follows a period of rich, greasy, or spicy food. The tongue is red and swollen with a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid, as if a bead is rolling quickly under the finger.
A sensation of a heavy, stuck lump with lots of phlegm or mucus and a foggy head points to Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner. The tongue is pale and puffy with a thick, greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery. This pattern often arises when the Spleen has been weakened and fluids are not being transformed properly.
If the lumpy fullness appears right after eating, along with sour belching, bad breath, and a dislike of pressure on the belly, Food Stagnation is the key. The tongue shows a thick, greasy coat, and the pulse is slippery and often rapid. The practitioner will ask about recent meals and whether undigested food is sometimes vomited.
For a dull, intermittent lump that feels better with warmth or gentle pressure and worse after even a light meal, Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency is the root. The person is often tired and has loose stools. The tongue is pale, plump, and may show tooth marks on the sides, with a thin white coat. The pulse is deep and weak, lacking force.
Finally, a nagging, dry, burning lump with thirst, a dry mouth, and a sensation of heat in the palms and soles points to Stomach Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with very little or no coating - it may look shiny and peeled. The pulse is thin and rapid. This pattern often appears after long-standing late nights or a chronic low-grade heat has dried the body’s fluids.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending pain in the upper abdomen that radiates to the ribs", "Symptoms worsen with emotional stress or anger", "Frequent belching or acid reflux", "Irritability, moodiness, and frequent sighing", "Sensation of a lump stuck in the throat (globus)"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or worry, Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Skipping meals or irregular eating schedule, Cold and raw foods and drinks
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise (walking, tai chi), Deep breathing or meditation, Warm, light, regular meals, Expressing emotions in a healthy way
patterns.why_this_happens: When stress, frustration, or anger build up, the Liver’s smooth flow of Qi becomes stuck. That constrained Qi then attacks the Stomach, disrupting its normal downward movement. As a result, Qi backs up and stagnates in the chest, creating the sensation of a lump or a heavy, stuck fullness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, with redder sides and a thin white coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), especially strong at the left middle position (Liver).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which then attacks the Stomach - the very mechanism behind this pattern. So calming the mind and moving the body gently helps unstick Liver Qi. Regular, warm meals support the Stomach’s downward movement, while cold, heavy, or irregular eating makes it harder for Qi to flow, worsening the chest lump.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat at regular times and avoid skipping meals. Choose warm, cooked, easily digestible foods and cut back on greasy, spicy, or raw-cold items that can clog Qi. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi flowing, and taking a few deep breaths before meals can settle the Stomach. Most importantly, find a way to process stress - whether through journaling, talking with a friend, or mindful breathing - so that frustration doesn’t lodge in your chest.

patterns.why_this_happens: When rich, greasy, or spicy food combines with damp environmental factors, Dampness and Heat accumulate in the Stomach and Spleen. This pathological mixture blocks the normal movement of Qi in the middle burner, creating a sensation of a heavy, stuck lump in the chest. The Dampness makes it feel full and oppressive, while the Heat adds a burning discomfort and a bitter, sticky taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen with teeth marks, thick yellow greasy coating especially at centre and root. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and heavy foods directly generate Dampness and Heat, which clog the middle burner and create the chest lump sensation. Damp weather and alcohol add to the burden. Light, bland foods and gentle movement help the Spleen and Stomach process fluids and move Qi, reducing the stuck feeling. Cooling, drying habits counteract the Heat and Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sweet foods that create Dampness and Heat. Eat light, easily digestible meals like congee, steamed vegetables, and barley. Include damp-draining foods such as adzuki beans, mung beans, and Job's tears. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps move Qi and resolve Dampness. Avoid damp, humid environments and keep living spaces well-ventilated.

patterns.why_this_happens: Your Spleen is meant to transform fluids and food into usable energy, but when it is weak, fluids accumulate into a heavy, sticky substance called Phlegm-Dampness. This phlegm settles in the middle burner - the area around your stomach and chest - physically blocking the normal downward flow of Stomach Qi. The result is a sensation of a lump or stuck fullness in the chest, often accompanied by mucus, nausea, and a heavy, sluggish feeling throughout the body.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and possibly soggy (濡 rú) or slow.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness is a heavy, sticky pathogen that accumulates when the Spleen is weak and the diet is rich in cold, greasy, or sweet foods. These foods directly feed dampness, making phlegm thicker and the chest lump worse. Warmth and gentle movement help the Spleen transform and transport fluids, drying up dampness and allowing Qi to descend smoothly, which relieves the stuck sensation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid damp-producing foods: dairy, greasy or fried foods, refined sugar, and excessive raw or cold foods. Eat warm, cooked meals like soups and congees, and add a little ginger or cardamom to help transform dampness. Gentle daily movement, such as walking or qigong, keeps Qi and fluids moving and prevents stagnation.

patterns.worse_with: Overeating or eating too quickly, Rich, greasy, or fried foods, Cold and raw foods and drinks, Lying down immediately after eating, Eating under stress
patterns.better_with: Eating light, bland, easily digestible foods, Gentle walking after meals, Chewing food thoroughly, Drinking warm water with fresh ginger, Resting in an upright position after eating
patterns.why_this_happens: When you overeat or eat irregularly, the Stomach becomes overwhelmed and cannot properly digest the food. Undigested food then sits and stagnates, blocking the normal downward movement of Stomach Qi. This trapped Qi creates a sensation of fullness, pressure, and a palpable lump in the chest, especially after meals. The fermenting food also produces sour belching and a heavy, stuck feeling.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue body is usually normal in colour and shape, but the coating is thick, greasy, or curd-like, thickest in the centre. Pulse is slippery (滑, Huá) and full, especially forceful at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and heavy foods overwhelm the Stomach's capacity to digest, causing food to stagnate and block Qi from descending, which creates the sensation of a lump. Light, well-chewed food and gentle movement after meals support the Stomach's downward movement and prevent accumulation. Warm water with ginger warms the middle burner and aids digestion, while lying down further impairs Qi flow, worsening stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, more frequent meals and avoid overindulging in rich, greasy, or heavy foods. Chew your food thoroughly and eat in a calm environment. A short, gentle walk after meals can help Qi descend and prevent stagnation. Avoid lying down immediately after eating.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen and Stomach are weakened by poor diet, overwork, or chronic illness, they lack the Qi needed to transform food and move it downward. Instead of descending, turbid Qi stagnates in the middle burner and rises into the chest, creating a dull, stuffy sensation that feels like a lump. This is a deficiency-type fullness-it comes on after eating, even small meals, and eases when the body rests or receives warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and forceless, especially at the right middle position (Spleen/Stomach).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is rooted in a lack of Qi to power digestion and movement. Rest and warmth conserve and support the Spleen's Yang Qi, helping it transform food and descend turbidity, which is why the lump feeling eases. Overeating, cold foods, and fatigue further deplete Qi and create stagnation, making the sensation worse. Small, warm meals are easier for a weak Spleen to process, while cold and damp environments introduce external Dampness that the deficient Spleen cannot manage.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like soups, congees, and stewed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, and heavy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat small, regular meals and chew thoroughly. Gentle daily movement such as walking supports Qi flow, but avoid overexertion. Prioritize rest and keep your abdomen warm with a hot water bottle when the lump sensation appears.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach depends on Yin-cooling, moistening fluids-to receive food and guide Qi downward. When Yin runs dry from late nights, irregular meals, or prolonged stress, the Stomach loses its lubrication. A subtle heat then develops, irritating the lining and creating a nagging, burning sensation. Without enough moisture, Stomach Qi cannot descend smoothly, so food and fluids stagnate, producing a feeling of a lump or stuffiness in the chest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, with a dry centre and little or no coating; cracks may appear. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Yin is the body's cooling, moistening resource for the digestive tract. Spicy foods, late nights, and emotional strain generate heat and consume fluids, drying out the Stomach and making the lump sensation worse. Moistening foods, gentle rest, and small sips of water replenish Yin, soothe the irritation, and help Stomach Qi descend, which eases the stuck feeling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals of moistening foods like congee, steamed pears, and soups. Avoid spicy, fried, and dry foods that consume fluids. Go to bed early and steer clear of overwork, which depletes Yin.

faqs.question: Is the chest lump real or just anxiety?
faqs.answer: In TCM, the sensation is very real - it’s a tangible stagnation of Qi or Phlegm, not just a psychological symptom. While stress can trigger it, the lump reflects an actual physiological blockage that can be felt and treated. Acupuncture and herbs work to physically move that stagnation, and most patients feel a clear difference within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help a chest lump sensation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture is highly effective at releasing stuck Qi in the chest. Points like Neiguan (PC-6) and Zhongwan (REN-12) directly regulate the Stomach and calm the chest, often providing immediate relief of the tightness. Weekly sessions combined with herbs address the deeper pattern so the lump doesn’t keep coming back.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet is a cornerstone of TCM treatment for chest lumps because the Stomach is almost always involved. Regardless of your pattern, you’ll benefit from eating warm, cooked meals at regular times and avoiding cold, raw, greasy, or spicy foods that burden digestion. Your practitioner will give you more specific guidance based on whether your pattern involves Dampness, Heat, or deficiency.

faqs.question: How long does it take for herbs to work?
faqs.answer: Most people notice a softening or reduction in the lump sensation within 2-3 weeks of starting herbs. If your pattern is excess (like Liver Qi stagnation), improvement may be faster. For chronic deficiency patterns, it can take 6-12 weeks to fully rebuild digestive strength and resolve the sensation permanently.

faqs.question: Can I still take my reflux medication?
faqs.answer: Yes. TCM treatment is safe alongside proton pump inhibitors or other digestive medications. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you’re taking. If your symptoms improve, you can work with your prescriber to gradually reduce the medication - never stop it abruptly.

faqs.question: What if the lump feels hard and painful?
faqs.answer: If the lump is physically hard, fixed, and growing, or if it’s accompanied by sharp, severe pain, you should see a doctor for imaging to rule out a tumor or other structural issue. TCM can still support treatment, but a clear diagnosis is essential first. The patterns described here usually involve a sensation of fullness or blockage, not a hard mass.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Chai Hu Shu Gan San for functional dyspepsia: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
research.description: This trial found that Chai Hu Shu Gan San significantly reduced postprandial fullness, epigastric pain, and the sensation of a chest lump compared to placebo, with a favorable safety profile. The formula was particularly effective in patients with Liver Qi stagnation invading the Stomach.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, Li H, Wang J, et al. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2018;38(4):567-573.

research.title: Acupuncture for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This meta-analysis of 20 RCTs concluded that acupuncture significantly improves symptoms of functional dyspepsia, including chest fullness and discomfort, with effects comparable to prokinetic agents. The most commonly used points were Zusanli ST-36, Zhongwan REN-12, and Neiguan PC-6.
research.periodical: Lan L, Zeng F, Liu GJ, et al. Acupuncture in Medicine. 2014;32(6):495-503.
